text: Yasha, the root of Jesus' name, carries the idea of ample space. Egypt, Mitzrayim, means double narrowness.
explanation:
In Hebrew, yasha (to save, rescue, deliver) is the verb behind Yeshua, Jesus. The lexicons note its root idea: to be wide, roomy, at large. Salvation is being brought into a spacious place. Affliction, by contrast, is being hemmed in, and Mitzrayim, Egypt, the house of bondage, literally means double straits.

"I called on the Lord in distress; the Lord answered me and set me in a broad place." When life feels cramped, with your movement, finances or options squeezed, remember whose name you call on. Jesus is the Lord of time and space, and enlarging is what His name does.

text: The spies stood in the Valley of Eshcol, "cluster." Ten saw giants; two saw the grapes. Which cluster do you see?
explanation:
"They came to the Valley of Eshcol, and there cut down a branch with one cluster of grapes; they carried it between two of them on a pole." Eshcol means cluster. All twelve stood in the same valley, holding the same fruit. Ten came back talking about giants; Joshua and Caleb talked about the land.

When the news is full of clusters of sickness, God can raise up clusters of blessing: homes and churches full of joy, healing and provision. And notice how that cluster was carried: crushed between two, hanging on a pole. Wine only comes from crushed grapes. Jesus was crushed on a cross between two men so that the blessing could flow to you.

text: In Hebrew, "to fight" (lacham) and "bread" (lechem) have the same letters. You fight by feeding.
explanation:
"Now Amalek came and fought with Israel." The word for fought is lacham, spelled exactly like lechem, bread, as in Bethlehem, the house of bread. Hidden inside the problem is the answer. Your weapon against the enemy is to feed: on the Word, on Christ, at His table.

"You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies." Not after they've gone. While the symptoms are still there, while the bills are still unpaid, God says, "Sit down and eat." Keep feeding on His word and partaking of His supper. You can eat your way through to the other side.

text: David's chief mighty man killed 800 in one battle. His name, Josheb-Basshebeth, means "he who sits in the seat."
explanation:
At the head of the list of David's mighty men is a warrior who "killed eight hundred men at one time." What was his secret? It's hidden in his name: Josheb-Basshebeth, the one who sits in the seat. The King James simply translates it, "the Tachmonite that sat in the seat."

God has "raised us up together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus." Rest isn't laziness; nobody was more at rest than Jesus, and nobody accomplished more. The one who sits accomplishes far more than the one who strives. Today that means not slaying 800, but saving them.

text: Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim, "resting places." The enemy's goal is to drive you from rest into anxious toil.
explanation:
Sometimes you're attacked not because you've done wrong but because you're at rest. Rephidim means resting places, and Amalek, whose name echoes amal, painful, stressful labor, came to drive Israel out of them. Mark says the disciples were "straining at rowing, for the wind was against them": hard work, good intentions, going nowhere.

When you notice worry, care and strain filling you, stop. "Be still, and know that I am God." The word is raphah, to let go, to relax, related to rapha, to heal. Labour isn't the problem; Paul worked harder than anyone, "yet not I, but the grace of God." Work, but from rest.

text: "They willingly received Him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land."
explanation:
The disciples were halfway across the lake, rowing hard against the wind, when Jesus came walking on the water. "It is I; do not be afraid." Literally, "I am." Mark says He would have passed them by. But they willingly received Him into the boat, and the wind ceased, and immediately they were at the shore they'd been straining toward.

They were already His disciples. Yet He waited to be welcomed in. Is there an area of your life you haven't willingly received Him into: your work, a relationship, a decision? Invite Him in. Wherever He's welcome, there's a timeless, spaceless quality. The struggle ends, and you arrive.

text: After a fire, a farmer nudged a charred hen, and her chicks ran out alive. That's how He covers you.
explanation:
After a wildfire swept through his farm, a farmer walked the ruins and found one of his hens burnt black beside the coop. He nudged her with his foot, and out from under her wings scurried her chicks, unharmed. She had covered them, and taken the fire herself.

Jesus wept over Jerusalem: "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were not willing!" He took the fire of judgment for you. "He shall cover you with His feathers, and under His wings you shall take refuge." Today, bring your family under His wings.
